w: 1 Attachment loss into the furcation drops the prognosis A professor's hint · 2 questions in the bank Know this From the recorded lecture; he repeated it all through. Once CAL reaches the furcation the prognosis falls, because the area is so hard to instrument and to clean. A furcation is a normal anatomical region of a multi-rooted tooth (premolars and molars) where the roots diverge from the root trunk, a finding as normal as a cusp tip. A furcation defect is what periodontal infection makes of it: destruction of the soft tissue and bone between the roots, seen as clinical attachment loss into the furcation. The point Dr. Litz called arguably the most important of the lecture, and repeated throughout: attachment loss that involves the furcation dramatically decreases the prognosis of the tooth. Furcations are extremely hard to instrument and even harder for the patient to clean, so check for them at every exam: the initial exam, routine prophy checks and periodontal maintenance. 2 Bower's furcation entrance depths from the CEJ A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Bower's entrance depths from the CEJ. Maxillary first molar: mesiopalatal ~3.6 mm, buccal ~4.2 mm, distopalatal ~4.8 mm. Mandibular first molar: buccal ~2.4 mm, lingual ~2.5 mm. A 4-5 mm probing depth may already mean an exposed furcation. Dr. Litz called these very important numbers to know (Bower, 1979), measured from the CEJ. Maxillary first molar: three entrances, the mesiopalatal about 3.6 mm, the buccal about 4.2 mm and the distopalatal about 4.8 mm. Another slide rounds these to about 3.5, 4 and 5 mm. Mandibular first molar: two entrances, buccal about 2.4 mm and lingual about 2.5 mm, significantly shorter than the maxillary ones, so a probing depth of 4-5 mm on a molar may already mean the furcation is exposed. (The class exam-review guide lists maxillary entrances of 3, 3.5 and 5 mm; the order is the same.) 3 The maxillary buccal furcation is affected most A professor's hint · 1 question in the bank Know this Maxillary molars are affected more than mandibular; on maxillary molars buccal > mesiopalatal > distopalatal; on mandibular molars the buccal is affected most. Multi-rooted teeth with short root trunks get furcation involvement after minimal attachment loss and often have a less favorable prognosis than single-rooted teeth or teeth with long trunks. Maxillary molars are affected more often than mandibular molars. On maxillary molars the buccal furcation is the most commonly affected, followed by the mesiopalatal and then the distopalatal. On mandibular molars, the buccal furcation is affected most. 4 Primary cause is plaque-driven attachment loss; cervical enamel projections and their grades A professor's hint · 6 questions in the bank Know this Plaque-driven periodontitis is the primary cause. CEPs, enamel pearls, overhangs, root form and trunk length are contributing factors. Cervical enamel projections: amelogenesis fails to halt before root formation; nothing attaches to enamel, so plaque is funneled into the furcation. ~30% of mandibular vs ~15% of maxillary molars, more on second molars and the buccal. The primary cause of furcation involvement is progressive clinical attachment loss from inflammatory periodontal disease, that is, plaque. He expects that question on every periodontal exam in dental school and on boards. Other factors contribute: Dr. Litz singled these out as a definite test question, and more important than that, something to know for life. A CEP is an apical projection of enamel from the CEJ that approaches or enters the furcation: a narrow, wedge-shaped extension (like a widow's peak) pointing from the CEJ toward the furcation. It forms when amelogenesis fails to halt before root formation. Because junctional epithelium and connective tissue can't attach to enamel, the gingiva lies over it without attachment, and the CEP acts like a funnel leading plaque straight into the furcation: a biologic weak link that lowers resistance to furcation involvement. CEPs are more common on mandibular molars (about 30%) than maxillary molars (about 15%), and more likely on second molars and on the buccal than the lingual, mesial or distal. 5 One deep site in a stable mouth: look for a local cause A professor's hint · 2 questions in the bank Know this One deep site on one tooth means a cause specific to that tooth: a CEP, an overhang, retained cement, a vertical root fracture. Repeated in class: one deep site in a stable mouth points to a local cause on that tooth (CEP, overhang, residual cement, or a vertical root fracture, which means extraction). Enamel pearls: balls of enamel, most common in the furcations of molars. Connective tissue can't attach to enamel and the pearl's shape holds plaque. On a radiograph, a radiopaque semicircle in the furcation suggests one. Small ones may be removed, usually with surgical access and a finishing bur. Treatment rests on one fact: new attachment will not form on enamel. If there is no bone or attachment loss with the CEP, often the case with Grades 1 and 2, usually no treatment is needed; watch it. If bone or attachment loss is associated with it, remove the CEP. Thin enamel comes off with a diamond or finishing bur (usually through a flap; sometimes without one if it's very shallow). If the enamel is thicker, removal can be attempted with care not to expose the pulp, and on a vital tooth, warn the patient about possible thermal sensitivity. His broader rule: a lone furcation involvement in an otherwise periodontally stable patient should prompt you to look for a CEP. One deep site on one tooth in a healthy mouth means something specific to that tooth (a CEP, an overhang, retained cement, a vertical root fracture on an endodontically treated tooth). 6 Furcation arrows, and the clinical exam before the radiograph A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this An arrow means involvement is highly likely, but no arrow rules nothing out: never the sole diagnostic tool. The Nabers probe is the best way to find a furcation. His rule for all of dentistry. Take periapicals and vertical bitewings; clinical exam alone found 3% / 9% of involved maxillary / mandibular molars, combined 65% / 23%. On radiographs, furcation bone loss can come from periodontitis, endodontic infection, root perforation or occlusal trauma. A mandibular molar's two roots make furcation bone loss easy to see. On maxillary molars it's harder because of superimposition: bone loss in the buccal furcation is often masked by the palatal root. Mesiopalatal and distopalatal lesions often show a furcation arrow, a small triangular radiolucency pointing into the furcation. About 30-55% of Grade II or III involvements show one. A furcation arrow on the film means furcation involvement is highly likely, but many involved furcations show none, so it must never be the sole diagnostic tool. His rule for all of dentistry: do the clinical exam first, reach a diagnosis, then use the radiographs to confirm it. Probing (perio probe and Nabers probe) gives the presence and extent of involvement, the attachment level relative to the furcation, and the extent and shape of the defect; radiographs give the interdental bone level and the bone within the root complex, and root shape. Take both periapicals and vertical bitewings. In one study (Ross and Thompson, 1980), clinical exam alone detected furcation involvement in only 3% of maxillary and 9% of mandibular molars; adding radiographs raised it to 65% of maxillary but only 23% of mandibular molars. Use both. 7 Osseous surgery: bone follows the gingiva, spare the furcation, debride the roots A professor's hint · 7 questions in the bank Know this The rationale for osseous surgery: gingiva is scalloped and returns to that shape after surgery, so the bone must be reshaped to follow it, or the pockets come back. The primary objective of osseous surgery is to eliminate periodontal pockets and create a shallow gingival sulcus the patient can keep clean, with a bony architecture that matches a physiologic gingival architecture. Gingiva is scalloped, like a child's drawing of ocean waves, higher interproximally and lower on the midfacial, and it returns to that shape after surgery even if the bone underneath does not. His most important slide: if the bone does not follow the overlying gingival architecture, the pockets will recur. Ochsenbein defined resective surgery as a procedure to eliminate bony deformities so that bone and gingiva are consistent with each other and the pocket is reduced or eliminated. Treating bone loss by removing bone sounds backwards, he said, but sometimes you fight fire with fire. Periodontitis leaves an uneven bone crest and deep pockets, especially where bone is lost vertically between teeth. In health, the interproximal crest sits about 1 to 2 mm from the adjacent CEJs on a radiograph. Normal alveolar bone has three features: the interproximal bone is more coronal than the labial or lingual bone and pyramidal; the shape of the interdental bone follows the tooth form and embrasure width; and the bony margin mimics the contour of the CEJ. In positive architecture the interproximal crest is coronal to its midfacial and midlingual height, the healthy pattern and the goal. In negative (reverse) architecture it is apical, a crater with deep pockets between the teeth. Flat architecture lies between. When reaching positive architecture would mean removing too much facial and lingual bone, as around a deep interproximal defect between #28 and #29, he settles for flat rather than weaken the tooth. 8 Ineffective plaque control is the first contraindication; the 1981 root planing study A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this The goal of Phase I and of surgery alike: shallow pockets the patient can clean. Surgery cures nothing on its own. Ineffective plaque control is the first contraindication to periodontal surgery, which is why the Phase I re-evaluation checks home care before anyone picks up a scalpel. The contraindications: ineffective plaque control, the big one ("there's not a periodontist on this earth that doesn't know this"), which the re-evaluation is there to catch, since surgery cures nothing and only creates an environment the patient can keep clean; noncompliance with the treatment plan, such as wanting to skip Phase I; shallow pockets, where surgery or root planing causes attachment loss; a hard-tissue defect amenable to regeneration, which should be regenerated instead (Session 6); an anticipated unacceptable cosmetic result, such as long maxillary anterior teeth in a patient with a high smile line; and uncontrolled systemic disease. 9 Furcation class from the Nabers probe, and the treatment by class Midterm check-ins · 3 questions in the bank Furcations are examined with the curved Nabers probe, inserted gently under the free gingival margin to feel for the entrance; it takes seconds. The Glickman classification (1953), the one Dr. Litz uses: Also flagged in class Grade 1: the CEJ dips toward the furcation. Grade 2: approaches but doesn't enter. Grade 3: enters the furcation. No bone or attachment loss: observe. Loss: remove it. The 1981 root planing study: residual calculus rises with pocket depth, which is the case for surgical access. Root debridement is the key step of any periodontal surgery, resective or regenerative: without clean roots nothing works. In osseous surgery around a molar, bone is removed on each root's facial and lingual, never in the furcation. You can skip Said of the step-by-step regeneration slides: know which patients and furcations are good candidates more than each step. Local antibiotics and resective surgery were left for their own lectures.
